claims.evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Neurons with less negative resting membrane potentials demonstrate higher burst frequencies and often generate 'ectopic' bursts not reflected in the XII output.
claims.source: Neurons with more negative resting membrane potentials usually generate bursting activity that is fully consistent with, and reflected in, XII output activity, whereas neurons with less negative resting membrane potentials demonstrate higher burst frequencies and often generate 'ectopic' busts not reflected in the XII output (see example in Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Pharmacological blockade of synaptic transmission within the pre-BötC by CNQX results in a reduction and desynchronization of neuronal activity within the pre-BötC, with no activity in the hypoglossal output.
claims.source: Pharmacological blockade of synaptic transmission within the pre-BötC by 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) results in a reduction and desynchronization of neuronal activity within the pre-BötC, with no activity in the hypoglossal output (see example in Figure 1C1,C2).
claims.evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1C1,C2.

claims.claim: The computational model of the pre-BötC consists of 100 neurons described in the Hodgkin-Huxley style, with sparse excitatory synaptic interconnections between neurons.
claims.source: we modeled the pre-BötC as an excitatory network consisting of 100 neurons described in the Hodgkin-Huxley style, with sparse excitatory synaptic interconnections between neurons.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational model structure used in the study.

claims.claim: The intrinsic bursting properties of neurons in the model were based on the persistent (slowly inactivating) sodium current, INaP.
claims.source: The intrinsic bursting properties of these neurons were based on the persistent (slowly inactivating) sodium current, INaP (Butera et al., 1999a; Butera et al., 1999b; Del Negro et al., 2001; Rybak et al., 2003a; Rybak et al., 2003b; Rybak et al., 2004; Rybak et al., 2014; Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010; Jasinski et al., 2013; see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the computational model, supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claims.claim: In the absence of coupling, the population contained silent neurons, as well as neurons with bursting and tonic activities.
claims.source: In the absence of coupling (when all weights of connections were set to zero), the population contained silent neurons, as well as neurons with bursting and tonic activities (Figure 2A1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2A1.

claims.claim: Neurons with the most negative EL values were silent.
claims.source: This figure shows that neurons with the most negative EL values were silent (neurons with ID numbers from 1 to 49)
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: Neurons with intermediate EL exhibited bursting activity with burst frequency increasing with EL.
claims.source: neurons with intermediate EL exhibited bursting activity with burst frequency increasing with EL (neurons 50–94)
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: Neurons with greatest EL displayed tonic spiking.
claims.source: and neurons with greatest EL displayed tonic spiking (neurons 95–100).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: The lack of network interactions resulted in asynchronous neuronal activity and the corresponding integrated population histogram lacked phasic modulation.
claims.source: The lack of network interactions resulted in asynchronous neuronal activity and the corresponding integrated population histogram lacked phasic modulation (Figure 2A3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2A3.

claims.claim: When relatively weak and sparse excitatory synaptic connections among neurons were incorporated in the model, the patterns of population activity and integrated output dramatically changed.
claims.source: The patterns of population activity and integrated output dramatically changed when relatively weak and sparse excitatory synaptic connections among neurons were incorporated in the model (Figure 2B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2B1-B3.

claims.claim: In the coupled case, overlapping clusters (sub-populations) of neurons with synchronized bursting generate MMOs characterized by alternating LA and SA population bursts.
claims.source: The raster plot of the same sorted neurons in this coupled case (Figure 2B2) shows the presence of overlapping clusters (sub-populations) of neurons with synchronized bursting, which generate MMOs characterized by alternating LA and SA population bursts (Figure 2B3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2B2-B3.

claims.claim: While the burst frequency increased with the neuronal excitability, the spike frequency within the burst changed in an inverse manner, i.e., decreased with increasing neuronal excitability.
claims.source: An important feature of all neurons operating in bursting mode is illustrated in Figure 3A3 (uncoupled case): while the burst frequency (blue curve) increased with the neuronal excitability (bottom-up), the spike frequency within the burst (red curve) changed in an inverse manner, i.e., decreased with increasing neuronal excitability.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model shown in Figure 3A3.

claims.claim: The reduction of spike frequency within the bursts in more excited neurons limited their ability to synchronize and recruit other neurons' activity in the coupled case.
claims.source: This reduction of spike frequency within the bursts in more excited neurons limited their ability to synchronize and recruit other neurons' activity in the coupled case (see below).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the computational model results.

claims.claim: Several clusters of neurons with synchronous bursting activity emerged dynamically in the coupled population.
claims.source: Several clusters of neurons with synchronous bursting activity emerged dynamically in the population.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: Clusters differed by the number of the population bursts in which they participated, which in turn defined the amplitude of integrated population bursts.
claims.source: Clusters differed by the number of the population bursts in which they participated (panel B1), which in turn defined the amplitude of integrated population bursts (panel C1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: Generation of low-frequency LA bursts involved synchronization of many neurons and included those with low excitability (most negative EL).
claims.source: Generation of low-frequency LA bursts involved synchronization of many neurons and included those with low excitability (most negative EL) (Figure 3B1,B2,C1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 3B1,B2,C1.

claims.claim: The sub-population of low excitability neurons do not contribute to SA bursts.
claims.source: Note that the sub-population of low excitability neurons, colored red, do not contribute to SA bursts.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: The sub-population of neurons with low excitability cannot be recruited by other sub-populations until sufficient recovery of bursting capability in the low excitability neurons has occurred.
claims.source: We further find that the sub-population of neurons with low excitability (colored red) cannot be recruited by other sub-populations (participating in SA bursts), and hence cannot generate LA bursts, until sufficient recovery of bursting capability in the low excitability neurons (defined by the INaP inactivation variable hNaP) has occurred.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model analysis.

claims.claim: The generation of LA bursts and the durations of their interburst intervals (IBIs) are mostly defined by the operation of an intrinsic burst-supporting mechanism in the less excitable neurons, rather than by variations in the intensity of their recruitment by the activity of highly excitable neurons involved in SA bursts.
claims.source: This observation suggests that with fixed parameter values, even though the low excitability neurons do not burst when uncoupled, the generation of LA bursts and the durations of their interburst intervals (IBIs) are mostly defined by the operation of an intrinsic burst-supporting mechanism in the less excitable neurons, rather than by variations in the intensity of their recruitment by the activity of highly excitable neurons involved in SA bursts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the computational model results.

claims.claim: When either weights or probability of connections were increased, the frequency of LA bursts increased and the number of SA bursts between successive LA bursts decreased.
claims.source: When either weights (Figure 4A1,A2,B1) or probability of connections (Figure 4A1,A3,B2) were increased, the frequency of LA bursts increased and the number of SA bursts between successive LA bursts decreased.
claims.evidence: This is a result from systematic parameter variations in the computational model shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: At the lowest weights (w = 1.0), only irregular SA bursts were observed because of insufficient neuronal synchronization.
claims.source: At the lowest weights (w = 1.0), only irregular SA bursts were observed because of insufficient neuronal synchronization (top trace, Figure 4B1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4B1.

claims.claim: No parameter sets produced stable regimes with more than five SA bursts per one LA burst.
claims.source: no parameter sets produced stable regimes with more than five SA bursts per one LA burst.
claims.evidence: This is a result from systematic parameter exploration in the computational model.

claims.claim: Simulations showed increased IBIs following the LA bursts, relative to IBIs observed after SA bursts, in all instances of MMOs.
claims.source: Furthermore, our simulations showed increased IBIs following the LA bursts, relative to IBIs observed after SA bursts, in all instances of MMOs (Figures 2B3,3C1, and 4B1,B2).
claims.evidence: This is a consistent result across multiple simulations shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: A reduced model was developed consisting of three neurons with mutual excitatory synaptic interactions.
claims.source: The model consisted of three neurons with mutual excitatory synaptic interactions (see Figure 5A1).
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the reduced model.

claims.claim: Each model neuron in the reduced model represented a sub-population of spiking neurons with a particular level of excitability.
claims.source: It was considered that each model neuron represented a sub-population of spiking neurons with a particular level of excitability.
claims.evidence: This describes the conceptual basis of the reduced model.

claims.claim: In the reduced model without coupling, neuron 1 (high excitability, HE) engaged in high frequency bursting, neuron 2 (moderate excitability, ME) engaged in low frequency bursting, and neuron 3 (low excitability, LE) was silent.
claims.source: EL values were distributed such that in the absence of coupling, neuron 1 (high excitability, HE) engaged in high frequency bursting, neuron 2 (moderate excitability, ME) engaged in low frequency bursting with no special frequency relation to the bursting of the HE neuron, and neuron 3 (low excitability, LE) was silent; the three neurons' summed activity provided a representation of network output (Figure 5B1,C1,D1,E1).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavior of the reduced model without coupling, shown in Figure 5B1.

claims.claim: When connection weights were progressively increased in the reduced model, the network underwent a series of regime transitions progressing from only SA bursts to only LA bursts.
claims.source: Similarly to the previous model, when connection weights were progressively increased, the network underwent a series of regime transitions progressing from only SA bursts (Figure 5B1,B2) to only LA bursts (Figure 5E1,E2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: LA bursts involved activation of all neurons and occurred exactly on the cycles when the LE neuron activated.
claims.source: As in the previous model, LA bursts involved activation of all neurons and occurred exactly on the cycles when the LE neuron activated (Figure 5C1,C2,D1,D2,E1,E2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: For each neuron, when it was silent, there was a level of synaptic input that caused its activation.
claims.source: A key point was that for each neuron, when it was silent, there was a level of synaptic input that caused its activation.
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: The level of synaptic input required for activation depended on the degree of INaP deinactivation in the neuron, quantified by hNaP, as well as on its excitability.
claims.source: This level depended on the degree of INaP deinactivation in the neuron, quantified by hNaP, as well as on its excitability.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: The LE neuron is activated if the trajectory rises above the left knee, or local maximum, of the V3-nullcline.
claims.source: The LE neuron is activated if the trajectory rises above the left knee, or local maximum, of the V3-nullcline (analogously to the sample trajectory in Figure 5B3).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5B3.

claims.claim: Incoming synaptic excitation lowers the V3-nullcline.
claims.source: Incoming synaptic excitation lowers the V3-nullcline (Figure 5C3,D3,E3), a well-known effect known as fast threshold modulation (Somers and Kopell, 1993)
claims.evidence: This is a known mechanism supported by citation and demonstrated in the reduced model.

claims.claim: If a synaptic input lowers the left knee below the current value of hNaP3, then the LE neuron is activated.
claims.source: If a synaptic input lowers the left knee below the current value of hNaP3, then the LE neuron is activated (e.g., Figure 5C3, marked with 'iv').
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5C3.

claims.claim: The activation of the LE neuron depends on the recovery of hNaP3 when input arrives, and hence on the rate of recovery of hNaP3 relative to the frequency of input arrival.
claims.source: Therefore, the activation of the LE neuron depends on the recovery of hNaP3 when input arrives, and hence on the rate of recovery of hNaP3 relative to the frequency of input arrival.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: When synaptic weights were increased, the correspondingly larger excitatory input moved the V3-nullcline to lower hNaP3 values, allowing activation of the LE neuron with less recovery time and hence with fewer input cycles.
claims.source: When synaptic weights were increased, the correspondingly larger excitatory input moved the V3-nullcline to lower hNaP3 values, allowing activation of the LE neuron with less recovery time (increase of hNaP3) and hence with fewer input cycles.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: A discrete number of activations of the HE and ME neurons is needed before hNaP3 recovers to a level from which the LE neuron can activate, which gives rise to the quantal nature of the MMO patterns.
claims.source: In all cases, a discrete number of activations of the HE and ME neurons is needed before hNaP3 recovers to a level from which the LE neuron can activate (Figure 5C3,D3,E3), which gives rise to the quantal nature of the MMO patterns (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic insight explaining the quantal nature of MMOs.

claims.claim: Critical connection weights that separate regimes correspond to tangencies to curves of knees for neurons.
claims.source: Critical connection weights that separate regimes correspond to tangencies to such curves.
claims.evidence: This is a mathematical insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: The transition from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes as w is decreased occurs when the ME neuron no longer can activate on every cycle.
claims.source: For example, the transition from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes as w is decreased occurs when the ME neuron no longer can activate on every cycle (Figure 5D1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5D1.

claims.claim: At the transitional weights from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes, the trajectory, projected to the (input2, hNaP2) plane, exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the ME neuron.
claims.source: At the transitional weights, the trajectory, projected to the (input2, hNaP2) plane, exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the ME neuron (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The transition from 1:2 to 1:4 occurs when the LE neuron no longer can activate on every second cycle.
claims.source: Similarly, the next transition, from 1:2 to 1:4, occurs when the LE neuron no longer can activate on every second cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: At the weights for the transition from 1:2 to 1:4, the projection of the trajectory to the (input3, hNaP3) plane exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the LE neuron.
claims.source: Thus, at the weights for this transition, the projection of the trajectory to the (input3, hNaP3) plane exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the LE neuron (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: A change in the excitability of the LE neuron alone could alter the V3-nullclines and hence change the frequency of the LA cycles within each quantal MMO rhythm without any change in the overall oscillation frequency of the 3-neuron population.
claims.source: In contrast to changes in connection weights, a change in the excitability of the LE neuron alone could alter the V3-nullclines (for all input levels) and hence change the frequency of the LA cycles within each quantal MMO rhythm without any change in the overall oscillation frequency of the 3-neuron population (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: An increase in the excitability of the HE neuron alone caused an increase of the SA burst frequency.
claims.source: On the other hand, an increase in the excitability of the HE neuron alone caused an increase of the SA burst frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: IBIs were longer after LA bursts than after SA bursts in the MMOs observed in the large-scale model.
claims.source: Another feature of the MMOs observed in our large-scale model is that IBIs were longer after LA bursts than after SA bursts.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model.

claims.claim: Stronger excitation pushes a neuron's V-nullcline, including its right knee, to lower hNaP values and hence causes the active phase to end with more INaP inactivation.
claims.source: Stronger excitation pushes a neuron's V-nullcline, including its right knee, to lower hNaP values and hence causes the active phase to end with more INaP inactivation (i.e., lower hNaP-coordinate).
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: A longer recovery period is needed before subsequent activation of the leading neuron when the active phase ends with more INaP inactivation.
claims.source: Thus, a longer recovery period is needed before subsequent activation of the leading neuron.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: On LA cycles, all neurons excite each other, which causes a maximal lowering of V-nullclines and subsequently yields the longest IBIs.
claims.source: On LA cycles, all neurons excite each other, which causes a maximal lowering of V-nullclines and subsequently yields the longest IBIs.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claims.claim: Quiescence could be induced in the LE and ME neurons after decreasing all excitabilities by 8%.
claims.source: Quiescence could be induced in the LE and ME neurons after decreasing all excitabilities by 8% (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: A similar regime of only SA bursts could be produced by decreasing weights of neuronal interconnections.
claims.source: A similar regime of only SA bursts could be produced by decreasing weights of neuronal interconnections (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The two key features formulated (reduction of spiking frequency within bursts with increasing burst frequency and dependence of after-burst recovery on burst amplitude) represent common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons with distributed excitability that extend across many different bursting mechanisms.
claims.source: Therefore the two key features formulated above, which are critical for generation of network-based MMOs, appear to represent common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons with distributed excitability that extend across many different bursting mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a generalization based on analysis of different bursting mechanisms.

claims.claim: A progressive suppression of INaP in the pre-BötC in vitro by riluzole should cause a transitional MMO regime before abolishing rhythmicity completely.
claims.source: We consider this result as a prediction for future experimental study, suggesting that a progressive suppression of INaP in the pre-BötC in vitro by its specific blocker, riluzole, should cause a transitional MMO regime before abolishing rhythmicity completely.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the computational model results.

claims.claim: The effects of Cd2+ could either attenuate neuronal excitability or reduce excitatory synaptic interconnections within the pre-BötC.
claims.source: We therefore suggest that the effects of Cd2+, a blocker of calcium currents, could either attenuate neuronal excitability or reduce excitatory synaptic interconnections within the pre-BötC, as seen in our simulations (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison of model results with experimental observations.

claims.claim: Neurons with low excitability, which generate low frequency bursting with high intra-burst spike frequency, recruit LA bursts by synchronizing the activity of many neurons in the network and therefore play a critical role in the generation of MMOs.
claims.source: Our simulations and analysis suggest that neurons with low excitability, which generate low frequency bursting with high intra-burst spike frequency, recruit LA bursts by synchronizing the activity of many neurons in the network and therefore play a critical role in the generation of MMOs.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion from the computational modeling and analysis.

claims.claim: Neurons with relatively high excitability (EL), and therefore with the high burst frequency (HE neurons), participated in some SA and all LA bursts.
claims.source: Specifically, neurons with relatively high excitability (EL), and therefore with the high burst frequency (HE neurons), participated in some SA and all LA bursts
claims.evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model analysis.

claims.claim: Neurons with the lowest excitability and the lowest burst frequency (LE neurons) participated only in LA bursts.
claims.source: whereas neurons with the lowest excitability and the lowest burst frequency (LE neurons) participated only in LA bursts.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model analysis.

claims.claim: LE neurons had the highest spike frequency within the bursts and could provide the strongest excitatory synaptic inputs to other neurons, resulting in the network-wide synchronization underlying the generation of LA bursts.
claims.source: Importantly, since LE neurons had the highest spike frequency (Figure 3B3) within the bursts, they could provide the strongest excitatory synaptic inputs to other neurons, resulting in the network-wide synchronization underlying the generation of LA bursts.
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the large-scale model analysis.

claims.claim: A mechanism intrinsic to the LE neurons and connected with their slow recovery is critically involved in the generation of LA bursts, defining their IBIs and the output burst frequency.
claims.source: This suggests that a mechanism intrinsic to the LE neurons and connected with their slow recovery is critically involved in the generation of LA bursts, defining their IBIs and the output burst frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model analysis.

claims.claim: The strong mutual excitation that occurs during an LA burst is responsible for the pause in activity of the tonic spiking neurons after an LA burst in the large-scale model.
claims.source: Interestingly, based on this analysis and previous work (Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010) we can infer that the strong mutual excitation, that occurs during an LA burst, is responsible for the pause in activity of the tonic spiking neurons after an LA burst in the large-scale model (Figure 3B2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the model analysis and prior work.

claims.claim: Both the prolonged IBI and the pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts rely on the synaptic excitation from the full collection of neurons in the network.
claims.source: Both the prolonged IBI and the pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts rely on the synaptic excitation from the full collection of neurons in the network
claims.evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the model analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of prolonged IBI and pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts can be taken as evidence that the least excitable neurons in the network are not recipients of feed-forward inputs but rather participate in the recurrent network structure.
claims.source: and thus their presence can be taken as evidence that the least excitable neurons in the network are not recipients of feed-forward inputs but rather participate in the recurrent network structure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about network structure based on model behavior.

claims.claim: MMOs were artificially evoked at a moderate level of neuronal excitability produced by elevation of [K+]out to 5–6 mM in the study by Kam et al., 2013.
claims.source: These MMOs were artificially evoked at a moderate level of neuronal excitability produced by elevation of [K+]out to 5–6 mM and were characterized by a series of SA bursts ('burstlets') alternating with single LA bursts that, in contrast to the burstlets, were able to trigger the rhythmic bursts in the hypoglossal motor output and hence defined the frequency of output oscillations.
claims.evidence: This describes experimental conditions from a cited study.

claims.claim: The study by Kam et al., 2013 established the quantal nature of MMOs emerging in the pre-BötC.
claims.source: This study established the quantal nature of MMOs emerging in the pre-BötC in these conditions (e.g., Figure 2 of Kam et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claims.claim: The computational study does not support the interpretation of MMOs in the pre-BötC as indicative of separate rhythm- and pattern-generating sub-networks.
claims.source: Our computational study does not support the interpretation of MMOs in the pre-BötC as indicative of separate rhythm- (burstlets) and pattern- (bursts) generating sub-networks.
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: A single, inseparable population of coupled excitatory neurons incorporating endogenous neuronal oscillators with distributed excitability can reproduce and is sufficient to explain the coexistence of burstlets and bursts in population rhythmic activity.
claims.source: The results of our present modeling study instead suggest that a single, inseparable population of coupled excitatory neurons incorporating endogenous neuronal oscillators with distributed excitability can reproduce, and is sufficient to explain, the coexistence of burstlets and bursts in population rhythmic activity (i.e., the MMOs described in this work).
claims.evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claims.claim: The activity of low-excitable neurons involved in generation of low frequency LA bursts synchronize the entire population activity, explicitly defining its output frequency.
claims.source: In contrast, in the interconnected single network considered here, the activity of low-excitable neurons involved in generation of low frequency LA bursts (attributed by Kam et al. to the 'pattern generating circuits') synchronize the entire population activity, explicitly defining its output frequency ('rhythm').
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model.

claims.claim: The intrinsic properties of low-excitable neurons, specifically the temporal characteristics of their recovery, define the output frequency of a rhythm generator.
claims.source: Therefore, the intrinsic properties of these low-excitable neurons, specifically the temporal characteristics of their recovery (see Figures 5D1,D2 and 6B), but not deletions of unknown origin, define the output frequency of a rhythm generator that interacts with other circuits to shape the CPG activity pattern.
claims.evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model analysis.

claims.claim: INaP has been found in pre-BötC neurons and the rhythmic bursting activity in the pre-BötC could be abolished by pharmacological blockade of this current.
claims.source: INaP has been found in pre-BötC neurons and the rhythmic bursting activity in the pre-BötC could be abolished by pharmacological blockade of this current (Del Negro et al., 2002a; Rybak et al., 2003a; Rybak et al., 2003b; Hayes et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental observations.

claims.claim: The critical role of INaP in the pre-BötC bursting has been debated.
claims.source: but its critical role in the pre-BötC bursting has been debated (Del Negro et al., 2002b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation indicating scientific debate.

claims.claim: Del Negro et al., 2005 suggested that INaP may be the primary rhythm-generating current up to postnatal day 4 or 5 (P4 or P5), after which ICAN is also expressed and strongly contributes to rhythm generation.
claims.source: Del Negro et al., 2005 suggested that INaP may be the primary rhythm-generating current up to postnatal day 4 or 5 (P4 or P5), after which ICAN is also expressed and strongly contributes to rhythm generation.

claims.claim: In bursting mechanisms based on Ca2+-dependent potassium, Ca2+-activated nonspecific, or Na+-dependent potassium currents, a functionally similar slow recovery is usually connected with operation of either the Ca2+ or Na+/K+ pumps.
claims.source: For example, in the case of intrinsic bursting mechanisms based on Ca2+-dependent potassium (IK(Ca2+)), Ca2+-activated nonspecific (ICAN), or Na+-dependent potassium (IK(Na+)) currents, involving intracellular accumulation of Ca2+ or Na+ ions, a functionally similar slow recovery is usually connected with operation of either the Ca2+ or Na+/K+ pumps (Ekeberg et al., 1991; el Manira et al., 1994; Wallén et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2009a; Ryczko et al., 2010; Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010; Jasinski et al., 2013; Rybak et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The conclusion that the two key features are common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons contradicts the opinion published by Feldman and Kam, 2015 that previous computational models reproducing MMOs are not valid because neuronal bursting is critically dependent on slow deactivation kinetics of INaP.
claims.source: This conclusion clearly contradicts a recently published opinion (Feldman and Kam, 2015) that previous computational models reproducing the MMOs observed in the pre-BötC (e.g., Butera et al., 1999b; Rybak et al., 2004) are not valid because the neuronal bursting in these models is critically dependent on slow deactivation kinetics of INaP.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of disagreement with a published opinion, supported by the modeling results.

results.result: The pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BötC) is a medullary region that generates rhythmic bursting activity in vitro and in vivo, and progressive increases in extracellular potassium concentration evoke mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) characterized by alternating large and small amplitude bursts. Similar patterns have been observed in pathological breathing conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C16-C24 establish the pre-BötC's role in respiratory rhythm generation through multiple experimental observations cited from prior work. The experimental evidence from slice preparations (C16-C17), the induction of MMOs by elevated K+ (C18-C22), and clinical observations (C23-C24) provide converging support for this foundational result.

results.result: MMOs emerge within heterogeneous excitatory neural networks through progressive neuronal recruitment and synchronization. The MMO pattern depends on distributed neuronal excitability, network connectivity parameters, and cellular bursting properties that include inverse relationships between burst frequency and intra-burst spike frequency, and dependence of recovery period on burst amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C7 represent the core findings from computational modeling. The demonstration that MMOs arise from network heterogeneity (C3) with specific dependencies on network parameters (C4) and critical cellular properties (C5-C6) is well-supported by systematic simulations shown in Figures 2-4. The identification of key features (C5-C6) is critical for the mechanistic explanation.

results.result: Experimental recordings show that pre-BötC neurons exhibit heterogeneous resting membrane potentials and bursting behaviors, with neurons at different excitability levels showing different relationships to XII output. Pharmacological blockade of synaptic transmission desynchronizes neuronal activity and abolishes XII output.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 describe experimental observations from prior work that motivate the modeling approach. The cited evidence (Figure 1B, C1, C2) and multiple references support the existence of neuronal heterogeneity and the importance of synaptic coupling, providing empirical foundation for the computational models.

results.result: A computational model of 100 Hodgkin-Huxley neurons with INaP-based bursting and distributed excitability (EL) shows that without coupling, neurons exhibit silent, bursting, or tonic behaviors depending on excitability, with asynchronous population activity. The distribution of behaviors follows the excitability gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 describe the large-scale model structure and baseline (uncoupled) behavior. The model specification is clearly documented (C29-C30, Table 1), and the uncoupled behavior (C31-C35) is demonstrated in Figures 2A and 3A, showing the expected relationship between excitability and neuronal state.

results.result: When sparse excitatory synaptic connections are added to the heterogeneous network, overlapping clusters of synchronized neurons emerge dynamically, generating MMOs with alternating LA and SA bursts. Low excitability neurons participate only in LA bursts and exhibit high intra-burst spike frequency but low burst frequency. The generation of LA bursts depends on intrinsic recovery mechanisms in low excitability neurons rather than recruitment intensity.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C45 describe the emergence of MMOs in the coupled network and identify the critical role of low excitability neurons. The raster plots and population histograms (Figures 2B, 3B-D) clearly demonstrate cluster formation, differential participation in SA vs LA bursts, and the inverse relationship between burst frequency and spike frequency (C38). The mechanistic insight about recovery-dependent LA burst generation (C44-C45) is supported by the analysis in Figure 3D.

results.result: Systematic variation of synaptic weights and connection probability shows that increasing either parameter increases LA burst frequency and decreases the number of SA bursts between LA bursts, with quantal transitions between MMO regimes. At very low weights, only irregular SA bursts occur. IBIs are consistently longer after LA bursts than after SA bursts across all MMO regimes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 describe parameter dependencies demonstrated in Figure 4. The heat maps (Figure 4A) and activity traces (Figure 4B) systematically show quantal regime transitions with parameter changes. The observation of longer IBIs after LA bursts (C49) is consistently shown across multiple figures (2B3, 3C1, 4B1-B2), providing robust support.

results.result: A reduced three-neuron model with different excitability levels (HE, ME, LE) reproduces the key features of the large-scale model. Without coupling, HE bursts at high frequency, ME bursts at low frequency, and LE is silent. With increasing synaptic weights, the network transitions through quantal MMO regimes from only SA bursts to only LA bursts, with LA bursts occurring when the LE neuron activates.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 describe the reduced model and its qualitative agreement with the large-scale model. Figure 5 demonstrates the model structure (A1), uncoupled behavior (B1), and regime transitions with increasing weights (C1-E1). The correspondence between LE activation and LA bursts (C56) is clearly shown across panels C-E.

results.result: Mathematical analysis of the reduced model reveals that LE neuron activation depends on whether synaptic input lowers the V-nullcline knee below the current hNaP value. The quantal nature of MMOs arises because a discrete number of HE/ME activations is needed for sufficient hNaP recovery in the LE neuron. Increasing synaptic weights allows LE activation with fewer input cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 provide the mechanistic explanation for quantal MMOs using phase plane analysis. The nullcline analysis in Figure 5B3-E3 clearly demonstrates the threshold mechanism (C59-C61) and the role of hNaP recovery (C62). The explanation for quantal transitions (C63-C64) is well-supported by the geometric analysis and is consistent with the simulation results in Figure 6A.

results.result: Transitions between quantal MMO regimes occur at critical connection weights corresponding to tangencies between the system trajectory and curves of nullcline knees. The 1:1 to 1:2 transition occurs when the ME neuron can no longer activate on every cycle, and the 1:2 to 1:4 transition occurs when the LE neuron can no longer activate on every second cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 provide mathematical characterization of regime transitions. The tangency analysis is demonstrated in Figure 6C-D, showing the geometric conditions for transitions. This provides rigorous mathematical support for the qualitative observations and explains the discrete nature of regime changes.

results.result: Changes in excitability of individual neuron types have distinct effects: increasing LE excitability changes LA burst frequency without affecting overall oscillation frequency, while increasing HE excitability increases SA burst frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 describe differential effects of changing excitability in specific neuron types. However, the text states 'data not shown' for both claims, meaning no figures or quantitative results are provided to support these assertions. While the claims are mechanistically plausible given the model structure, they lack direct empirical support within the manuscript.

results.result: The reduced model explains why IBIs are longer after LA bursts: stronger excitation during LA bursts pushes V-nullclines to lower hNaP values, causing the active phase to end with more INaP inactivation, requiring longer recovery before subsequent activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 provide mechanistic explanation for the IBI differences observed in both models. The observation (C72) is supported by data in multiple figures. The mechanistic explanation (C73-C75) is supported by the phase plane analysis and the demonstration in Figure 6B showing different loop sizes for SA vs LA bursts in the HE neuron.

results.result: Reducing neuronal excitability by 8% or decreasing synaptic weights can eliminate LA bursts, leaving only SA bursts, with the LE and ME neurons becoming quiescent.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 describe manipulations that eliminate LA bursts, demonstrated in Figure 7A-B. Both manipulations produce qualitatively similar outcomes (only SA bursts), supporting the interpretation that either reduced excitability or reduced coupling can prevent LE neuron recruitment.

results.result: The two key features critical for MMO generation (inverse relationship between burst and spike frequency, and voltage-dependent recovery) are not specific to INaP-based bursting but represent common properties of most intrinsic bursting mechanisms, including those based on Ca2+- or Na+-dependent currents with pump-mediated recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C99-C101 generalize the findings beyond INaP-based mechanisms. While the models use INaP (C99), the authors provide strong theoretical arguments and extensive citations (C101) showing that similar properties arise from other bursting mechanisms. This generalization is well-reasoned and supported by knowledge of bursting dynamics, though not directly tested in the manuscript.

results.result: The model predicts that progressive suppression of INaP by riluzole should produce a transitional MMO regime before abolishing rhythmicity. The effects of Cd2+ in eliminating LA bursts could result from either reduced excitability or reduced synaptic connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are explicitly presented as predictions and hypotheses for future work. C79 is based on simulations in Figure 4B3 showing MMO emergence during INaP suppression, providing some support. However, C80 is more speculative, offering two alternative explanations for Cd2+ effects without definitive evidence to distinguish them. These require experimental validation.

results.result: Low excitability neurons play a critical role in MMO generation by synchronizing network activity during LA bursts. These neurons have the highest intra-burst spike frequency, participate only in LA bursts, and their intrinsic recovery properties define LA burst timing and output frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 synthesize key mechanistic insights from both models. The differential participation of neuron types (C82-C83) is clearly shown in Figures 3B-C. The high spike frequency of LE neurons (C84) is demonstrated in Figure 3B3. The critical role of LE recovery in determining LA burst timing (C85) is supported by analysis in both models (Figures 3D, 5-6).

results.result: Strong mutual excitation during LA bursts causes pauses in tonic spiking neurons and prolonged IBIs. These features indicate that low excitability neurons participate in recurrent network structure rather than receiving feed-forward inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 draw inferences about network structure from observed dynamics. The pause in tonic neurons after LA bursts (C86) is shown in Figure 3B2 and explained by prior work (Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010). The inference about recurrent vs feed-forward structure (C88) is logically sound given that the effects depend on full network activation (C87).

results.result: The computational study challenges the interpretation that MMOs in pre-BötC indicate separate rhythm- and pattern-generating sub-networks. Instead, a single heterogeneous population with distributed excitability can explain MMOs, with low-excitability neurons synchronizing population activity and their recovery properties defining output frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 present a key conceptual contribution, contrasting the current findings with the 'burstlet concept' of Kam et al. (2013) and Feldman and Kam (2015). The modeling results (C92) clearly demonstrate that a single network can produce MMOs. The mechanistic explanation (C93-C94) is well-supported by the analysis. This represents a substantive reinterpretation of experimental observations, though it remains a computational prediction requiring experimental validation.

results.result: While the role of INaP in pre-BötC bursting has been debated, all available MMO data were obtained from neonatal animals (P0-P5) within the developmental range where INaP is considered the primary rhythm-generating current, supporting its inclusion in the models.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 provide justification for the modeling choice to use INaP. The existence of debate (C96) and alternative hypotheses (C97) are acknowledged through citations. The argument that experimental MMO data come from the appropriate developmental stage (C98) is well-supported by citations and provides reasonable justification for the modeling approach.

results.result: The conclusion that key MMO-generating features are common across bursting mechanisms contradicts the opinion of Feldman and Kam (2015) that previous computational models are invalid due to dependence on slow INaP deactivation kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 explicitly addresses a criticism from Feldman and Kam (2015). The rebuttal is well-supported by the demonstration that the critical features (C78, C100-C101) are not specific to INaP kinetics but arise from general properties of bursting mechanisms. This represents a substantive contribution to ongoing scientific debate.

results.result: MMOs are characterized by alternating large and small amplitude oscillations and have been observed in multiple neural systems including entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, dopaminergic neurons, pre-BötC, and motoneurons. Heterogeneity is a ubiquitous property of central pattern generator circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 provide background context from prior literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to experimental observations (C9-C14) and reviews (C8, C15). These establish the broader significance of MMOs and heterogeneity in neural circuits, motivating the current study.
